Baby & Child

Growth and puberty in girls: what the timing can tell you

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Parents often wonder whether a first period means their daughter has stopped growing. Usually some growth remains, but the most rapid increase in height has already happened. The useful guide is the young person’s own growth and development over time, rather than a fixed age, shoe size or adult-height target.

There is no single birthday when growth stops

A child’s height changes rapidly in infancy, more steadily through much of childhood, and faster again during puberty. You may notice the change through shorter trousers, tighter shoes or a different position on the family height chart. Appetite, sleep or mood alone cannot tell you that a growth spurt is happening.

For girls, the fastest pubertal increase in height usually occurs before the first period. Growth then slows rather than stopping suddenly. One girl may be near her adult height while a same-age friend still has substantial growth ahead, because their puberty began at different times. Neither a sixteenth birthday nor a particular target height establishes that development is complete.

Puberty usually begins before the first period

Breast budding is commonly the first sign of puberty, usually beginning between ages eight and thirteen. The timing varies, and there is no ideal age that every child should match. The first period generally follows about two to three years after breast development begins; in the United States, the average age is around twelve.

Height often accelerates during the interval between breast budding and the first period, with the fastest growth commonly occurring before menstruation starts. A yearly growth figure needs the child’s age, stage and earlier measurements for interpretation. An estimate such as ten centimetres in a year should not become a requirement that every healthy child must meet.

Several body changes unfold at different speeds

Breast tissue, the areola and the nipple change gradually. One side may develop before the other, and some tenderness can occur. Hips and body composition also change. The external genital tissues, uterus and ovaries mature as part of puberty, but outward appearance cannot precisely reveal how much height growth remains.

Underarm and pubic hair can become darker and coarser over time. Hair growth and body odour do not always begin at the same time as breast development, because different hormonal processes contribute. Oily skin, acne and more noticeable sweating are also common. These changes are useful topics for practical, age-appropriate conversations, rather than a checklist a parent needs to inspect.

Growing feet are a clue, not a height prediction

Changing shoe size can be noticeable before the fastest increase in overall height. Researchers have studied this relationship, including a 2009 study of foot and height growth around pubertal onset and studies published in 2011. The findings suggest that foot growth can be an early population-level marker of development.

One 2011 study used shoe-shop records from 242 girls and 104 boys. Its authors noted that direct comparison of an individual child’s shoe-size changes and sitting-height growth was still needed to validate prediction. Another study examined foot length and pubertal maturation in 973 children. These studies do not establish that every girl reaches adult shoe size at twelve or that a parent can calculate final height from shoes.

Some height growth usually continues after the first period

The first period marks a point at which the most rapid height growth has generally already passed. The American Academy of Pediatrics describes another one to two inches, roughly 2.5 to 5 centimetres, as common afterward, with larger gains less common. This is a broad description, not a maximum or a promise for one child.

Remaining growth depends on the stage of skeletal maturation and the individual’s earlier pattern. There is not usually a separate second growth spurt caused by menstruation. Breast development and other physical changes can continue after height growth has slowed. A first period, fuller hips or a more mature-looking face cannot independently establish adult height.

Food, body composition and activity affect the wider picture

Growing bodies need enough energy and a varied supply of nutrients. Undernutrition, restrictive eating or a mismatch between food intake and the demands of intensive training can slow growth or delay puberty. Being active is not itself a disease, and a young athlete should not be assumed to have a problem without reviewing their health, training and nutrition together.

Higher body fat is associated with earlier pubertal development in some populations, but body size does not determine the timing for every child. Weight gain and changes in fat distribution are also ordinary parts of puberty. Avoid using food restriction, forced weight change or supplements to try to control the date of the first period or achieve a chosen height.

A clinician or appropriately qualified dietitian can help if meals have become stressful, the child is losing weight, tiredness is persistent or periods stop. The aim is adequate nourishment and health, not assigning blame to the child or family.

Family patterns matter, but they are not the whole story

Height is strongly influenced by many inherited factors. Parents who are shorter or taller than average often have children with a related pattern, but the outcome is not an exact copy of either parent. The timing of puberty can also run in families. A healthy late maturer may continue growing after peers have slowed down.

Some genetic conditions affect stature differently. Down syndrome is often associated with shorter height, while Marfan syndrome can include taller stature and longer limbs. These examples do not mean that a short or tall child probably has either condition. Clinicians consider the complete history, examination and, when relevant, condition-specific growth references.

Hormonal and chronic conditions can influence growth

The thyroid and pituitary glands contribute to normal growth and development. An underactive thyroid or problems with pituitary signals, including growth hormone or the signals that stimulate the ovaries, can affect height gain or puberty. Some ovarian conditions can delay development as well. Symptoms and growth measurements guide which possibilities need investigation.

Chronic conditions such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, cystic fibrosis, inflammatory bowel disease and poorly controlled diabetes can interfere with growth through inflammation, nutrition, metabolic effects or treatment factors. Having one of these conditions does not mean growth will inevitably be poor. Good disease control and monitoring are important, and growth changes may occasionally help reveal an illness before other symptoms are obvious.

Look at a growth record, not a classmate comparison

A single height measurement says little about growth speed. Measurements taken accurately over time can be plotted on an appropriate growth chart, showing whether the child broadly follows a pattern or begins to cross down through percentiles. A shorter child who is steadily following their curve can be different from a previously average-height child whose growth has slowed.

Bring earlier clinic measurements and relevant family growth history to an appointment. Home measurements can be useful if made consistently, but small differences in technique can create apparent changes. Daily measuring usually adds worry without useful information.

Slower growth over the past year or two and time since the first period can contribute to a clinical estimate of maturity. Pubic hair, breast appearance or losing a round childhood face are not reliable home tests. An intimate examination, if needed, should be explained and performed with consent, privacy and appropriate support.

Know when to ask for assessment

Discuss pubertal changes before age eight, no breast development by thirteen, or no first period by fifteen with a clinician. The time since breast development began also matters; do not wait for a birthday if progress appears to have stalled. These thresholds identify reasons to assess, not diagnoses to make at home.

Arrange review for a marked slowing of growth, unexplained weight change, persistent tiredness, chronic bowel symptoms or other new health concerns. A child who has begun menstruating and then goes more than three months without a period also needs advice. Pregnancy possibility is considered respectfully when relevant, alongside other causes.

An assessment may begin with history, a growth-chart review and examination. Selected blood tests or a hand and wrist X-ray for bone age may help answer a specific question. Bone age estimates skeletal maturity and can inform remaining-growth estimates, but it cannot provide a perfectly certain final height. Not every child needs testing or hormone treatment.

Support the young person as well as the growth chart

Puberty can bring embarrassment, social pressure and a stronger wish for independence. Mood changes are not a reason to dismiss persistent sadness, anxiety, withdrawal or conflict as unavoidable hormones. Offer calm opportunities to talk, and make a trusted adult or a private healthcare conversation available if your child prefers that.

Practical help can include comfortable clothes, a well-fitting bra if wanted, gentle skin care and menstrual supplies before the first period. Avoid teasing or repeatedly comparing bodies and heights. Ask what would make the changes easier to manage rather than turning development into a performance goal.

There is no supplement or exercise routine that guarantees extra centimetres beyond an individual’s growth potential. When a treatable condition is found, care is directed at that condition. Otherwise, good nutrition, ordinary activity, sleep and supportive follow-up help a child grow and develop without making height the measure of their wellbeing.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The fastest height growth generally precedes the first period; later growth is slower and varies between individuals.

Growth charts, clinical history and sometimes bone age or selected tests help assess concerns about early, delayed or interrupted development.

How BeMama can help

Keep previous height measurements and a brief family puberty history, and give your child space to ask questions privately.

When to seek help

Arrange assessment for pubertal changes before eight, no breast development by thirteen, no first period by fifteen, or a marked slowing of growth. Persistent distress or restrictive eating also deserves support.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • There is no universal age or height at which all girls finish growing.
  • A first period does not trigger a second growth spurt.
  • Shoe-size studies cannot reliably predict one child’s final height.
  • Nutrition, family patterns, hormones and chronic health all matter.
  • Respectful clinical assessment is more useful than inspecting development at home.

Frequently asked questions

Does height stop changing on the day of the first period?

No. Some growth usually continues, but it tends to be slower because the fastest pubertal growth has already occurred.

How much taller might a girl grow after her first period?

Another one to two inches, about 2.5 to 5 centimetres, is commonly described, but there is substantial individual variation. It is not a personal prediction or a fixed maximum.

Is there a second growth spurt after menstruation starts?

Not usually. The first period occurs after height growth has begun to slow; it does not initiate a separate new spurt.

Does every girl reach adult height at sixteen?

No. Puberty timing and skeletal maturation vary. A birthday alone does not establish that growth is complete.

Can larger shoes predict final height?

No. Studies link foot growth with puberty in groups, but shoe size cannot reliably calculate one child’s remaining growth or adult height.

Does playing sport delay puberty?

Ordinary activity does not automatically delay development. Very intensive training with insufficient energy intake can contribute, so the whole health and nutrition picture matters.

When should delayed puberty be checked?

Ask about no breast development by thirteen or no first period by fifteen, and earlier if development stalls or other symptoms appear. The clinician also considers time since breast budding.

What does a bone-age X-ray tell us?

It estimates skeletal maturity and can help assess growth potential. It is one part of the evaluation and cannot guarantee an exact adult height.

Should parents inspect body hair or breasts to judge growth?

No home inspection is needed to predict height. Discuss concerns with a clinician, who can explain any appropriate examination and respect the young person’s privacy.

Can vitamins or stretching guarantee extra height?

No. Treating a true deficiency or medical condition may help health and growth, but supplements and exercises do not guarantee additional height beyond individual potential.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
